misconception_pool.misconception: Athletes only face dehydration in hot summer weather during the running segment.
misconception_pool.fact: Multisport activities require structured prevention plans that address environmental exposure, traffic control, and physical trauma across all disciplines.

misconception_pool.misconception: Popping a friction blister with an unsterilized pin right before the run segment speeds up skin healing.
misconception_pool.fact: Intact skin over a blister acts as a sterile barrier against bacteria, so leave small blisters unbroken and pad them with moleskin.

misconception_pool.misconception: Drinking plain water as fast as possible is the safest treatment for an athlete showing confusion from heatstroke.
misconception_pool.fact: Heatstroke victims may have an altered mental state and choke on fluids, so focus on rapid external cooling and call emergency services.

misconception_pool.misconception: Muscle cramps during a long bike leg are caused strictly by lactic acid buildup and require immediate static stretching.
misconception_pool.fact: Exercise-associated cramps stem from neuromuscular fatigue and electrolyte loss, requiring reduced pace, gentle stretching, and sodium intake.

misconception_pool.misconception: Hypothermia only threatens multisport athletes when the ambient air temperature drops below fifty degrees Fahrenheit.
misconception_pool.fact: Water conducts heat away from the body roughly twenty-five times faster than air, causing hypothermia even in mild weather.

misconception_pool.fact: The cycling leg covers the longest distance and largest time proportion in most triathlons, followed by the run and then the swim.

misconception_pool.misconception: Proficient swimmers can conduct open water multisport training alone without surface safety watchers.
misconception_pool.fact: Safe Swim Defense mandates qualified adult supervision and trained lifeguards before any aquatic training session.

misconception_pool.misconception: Cyclists and runners share the exact same road rule and should both travel facing oncoming vehicular traffic.
misconception_pool.fact: Bicycles operate as vehicles and must ride with the flow of traffic on the right, while pedestrians run facing oncoming traffic.

misconception_pool.misconception: A bicycle helmet worn tilted back to expose the forehead still provides full impact protection during a crash.
misconception_pool.fact: A helmet must sit level just two finger-widths above the eyebrows so the foam shell absorbs frontal impact forces in a forward fall.

misconception_pool.misconception: Pool swimming skill guarantees safe open-water performance without needing lookouts or a designated buddy system.
misconception_pool.fact: Open water introduces currents, cold shock, and limited visibility, requiring all eight points of Safe Swim Defense and active lifeguards.

misconception_pool.misconception: Squeezing one brake lever halfway to the handlebar confirms both brakes and tires are ready for a race course.
misconception_pool.fact: A full pre-ride check requires verifying tire sidewall pressure, spinning both wheels for clearance, and testing front and rear brakes.

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: During the swim-to-bike and bike-to-run transitions in a triathlon, what rule applies to handling your CPSC-approved cycling helmet?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: During the swim-to-bike and bike-to-run transitions in a triathlon, what rule applies to handling your CPSC-approved cycling helmet?
options: A. You may unrack the bike first and buckle your helmet chin strap while coasting through the transition exit chute.
B. Your helmet must be on your head with the chin strap securely buckled before you unrack or touch your bike.
C. A helmet is only required on road courses with hills steeper than five percent and is optional inside the transition zone.
D. You should leave the chin strap unbuckled for the first mile after the swim so water can drain from your ears.
choices: A. You may unrack the bike first and buckle your helmet chin strap while coasting through the transition exit chute.
B. Your helmet must be on your head with the chin strap securely buckled before you unrack or touch your bike.
C. A helmet is only required on road courses with hills steeper than five percent and is optional inside the transition zone.
D. You should leave the chin strap unbuckled for the first mile after the swim so water can drain from your ears.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Your helmet must be on your head with the chin strap securely buckled before you unrack or touch your bike, and it must stay buckled until the bike is re-racked.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Multisport safety rules require athletes to put on and securely buckle a CPSC-approved helmet before touching or unracking the bicycle in T1 and to keep it buckled until the bike is fully racked in T2.
